did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a universal call: not only the peoples and nations are summoned to listen, but also the earth, the world, and all its inhabitants. Thus, the judgment described in the chapter is presented as an event of cosmic scope.

The description of the judgment uses vivid cosmic imagery: the host of heaven wastes away, the heavens are rolled up like a scroll, and their host withers like a leaf. These images emphasize the upheaval’s overwhelming power, not merely the destruction of a single kingdom.

The LORD’s sword is described in sacrificial language: it is “filled with blood” and “made fat with fat.” The destruction in Edom is called “a sacrifice to the LORD” and “a great slaughter” in the land of Edom.
Edom becomes the tangible focus of judgment in the chapter: the sword descends upon it, and it is called “the people under the ban”—a people devoted to destruction as part of divine judgment.
The destruction is presented not only as vengeance but also as “a year of recompense”—a time of repayment and retribution—and is explicitly connected with “the cause of Zion.”
The land’s transformation into a wasteland is described through an image of extreme disaster: streams turned into pitch, dust turned into sulfur, and the land burning with pitch.

After the destruction, the land is described in terms of “chaos” and “emptiness.” The use of a measuring line of chaos and stones of emptiness portrays the wasteland as though it were being carefully surveyed and marked out.

The palaces and fortresses are not merely destroyed; they become covered with wild plants and turn into a dwelling place for animals and birds. In this way, the royal domain is replaced by a wild landscape.

The prophet directs the reader to “the book of the LORD” and emphasizes that not one of the creatures will be missing and that none will lack its mate. This reference reinforces the claim that the entire vision is fulfilled precisely.

At the end of the chapter, the animals do not merely invade the desolate land: the LORD casts lots for them and apportions the land to them by line. They are destined to possess it and dwell there from generation to generation.
